questions.prompt: Why is the O−H proton of CH3COOH much more acidic than the O−H proton of CH3CH2OH?
options: Acetic acid contains more total hydrogen atoms
Ethanol cannot form any conjugate base
Acetate has no net negative charge
The carboxylate conjugate base delocalizes negative charge over two oxygens.
questions.explanation: D is correct. Resonance stabilization favors formation of acetate relative to the more localized ethoxide ion. A is incorrect: ethanol actually has more, and total hydrogen count does not establish acidity. B is incorrect: it can lose an O−H proton to form ethoxide, although much less readily. C is incorrect: resonance distributes the charge but does not remove its net value.

questions.prompt: ClCH2COOH is more acidic than CH3COOH. Which structural explanation is most appropriate?
options: Chlorine donates its proton to water
Chlorine withdraws electron density inductively and stabilizes the carboxylate conjugate base.
The C−Cl bond must break in every acid ionization
The extra atom makes every molecule with chlorine a strong acid
questions.explanation: B is correct. An electron-withdrawing substituent near the acidic group helps stabilize the anionic product. A is incorrect: the acidic proton is on the carboxyl O−H group, not chlorine. C is incorrect: proton transfer does not require cleavage of that bond. D is incorrect: substituent identity and position matter; chlorine alone does not guarantee strong acidity.

questions.prompt: Two otherwise similar carboxylic acids have a chlorine substituent close to or several bonds away from the COOH group. Which trend is expected from induction?
options: The farther chlorine must always have the larger effect
Position cannot affect acidity
The closer chlorine generally gives greater acid strengthening.
Both lose a proton from chlorine rather than oxygen
questions.explanation: C is correct. The electron-withdrawing inductive effect decreases with distance through bonds. A is incorrect: the through-bond inductive influence weakens with distance. B is incorrect: substituent distance can change conjugate-base stabilization. D is incorrect: neither structure has the acidic proton on chlorine.

questions.prompt: For the similar oxyacids HOCl and HOBr, why is HOCl the stronger acid?
options: The more electronegative Cl withdraws electron density and better stabilizes the conjugate base.
The H atom is bonded directly to Cl in HOCl
Cl is less electronegative than Br
HOCl is stronger because every chlorine compound is ionic
questions.explanation: A is correct. With the same H−O−X framework and oxygen count, central-atom electronegativity supports the trend. B is incorrect: it is bonded to oxygen. C is incorrect: the stated electronegativity trend is reversed. D is incorrect: HOCl is molecular and the structural comparison concerns conjugate-base stability.

questions.prompt: Why does adding oxygen atoms generally increase acid strength in an oxyacid series with the same central atom and the acidic H bonded to oxygen?
options: It necessarily increases the number of acidic hydrogens
Additional oxygens withdraw electron density and help stabilize the conjugate base.
It makes the conjugate base more eager to accept a proton
It eliminates all O−H bonds before dissolution
questions.explanation: B is correct. Inductive withdrawal and charge delocalization favor deprotonation in the higher-oxygen oxyacids. A is incorrect: oxygen addition need not add any hydrogen. C is incorrect: greater conjugate-base stability corresponds to weaker basicity. D is incorrect: the acid still contains its proton before ionization.

questions.prompt: HI is a stronger acid in water than HF despite F being more electronegative. Which factor explains this down-group comparison?
options: The H−F bond is weaker than the H−I bond
HF has no hydrogen capable of transfer
Iodide must be a stronger base than fluoride
The weaker H−I bond and the large, polarizable iodide conjugate base favor proton loss.
questions.explanation: D is correct. Bond strength changes down the group can outweigh an electronegativity-only argument for these binary acids. A is incorrect: the relevant bond-strength trend is opposite. B is incorrect: HF can donate a proton but does so incompletely in water. C is incorrect: the conjugate base of the stronger acid is weaker.

questions.prompt: Which structural feature lets NH3 act as a Brønsted base toward hydronium?
options: The nitrogen lone pair can form a bond to an incoming proton.
An N−H bond must release an electron to become metallic
NH3 contains a pre-existing hydroxide ion
Nitrogen must gain an additional lone pair before any proton can bind
questions.explanation: A is correct. Proton acceptance converts NH3 to NH4+ using its available electron pair. B is incorrect: acid-base proton transfer is not metal formation. C is incorrect: it is a molecular base and produces hydroxide by reacting with water. D is incorrect: its existing lone pair provides the required pair.

questions.prompt: Which proton in CH3C(=O)OH is most readily lost in its ordinary aqueous weak-acid behavior?
options: Any methyl C−H proton equally readily
A proton attached to the carbonyl oxygen that is not present in the written structure
The proton on the O−H bond.
No proton, because all carboxylic acids are non-acidic
questions.explanation: C is correct. Its loss gives resonance-stabilized carboxylate; removing a methyl C−H proton is much less favorable. A is incorrect: those removals do not give the same conjugate-base stabilization. B is incorrect: the neutral structure has its O−H proton on the hydroxyl oxygen. D is incorrect: carboxylic acids are a common weak-acid class.

questions.prompt: Perchloric acid is strong in water, whereas acetic acid is weak. Which comparison of their conjugate bases is consistent with conjugate stability?
options: ClO4− is a much weaker proton acceptor than CH3COO−.
ClO4− must be the stronger base because it contains more oxygen atoms
Both bases must be equally strong because they carry−1 charge
CH3COO− cannot accept a proton because it has resonance
questions.explanation: A is correct. The very stable conjugate base of a strong acid has little tendency to recapture a proton from water. B is incorrect: oxygen count alone does not imply stronger proton acceptance. C is incorrect: net charge alone does not specify base strength. D is incorrect: resonance stabilizes acetate but does not prevent its weak basicity.

questions.prompt: Why can OH− accept a proton more readily than H2O in their conjugate relationship?
options: OH− has no electron pairs and accepts a proton without bonding
Its negative charge and available oxygen electron density favor formation of neutral H2O.
H2O and OH− must have equal basicity because both contain oxygen
OH− is basic only because it contains two oxygens
questions.explanation: B is correct. Protonation of hydroxide relieves its negative charge, making it a much stronger base than neutral water. A is incorrect: oxygen electron pairs participate in the bond. C is incorrect: charge and bonding environment differ. D is incorrect: hydroxide contains one oxygen.

questions.prompt: For a typical diprotic acid H2A, the second proton is less readily removed from HA− than the first from neutral H2A. Which structural-charge argument supports this trend?
options: Each deprotonation always increases acid strength
HA− has no hydrogen left
The second proton is removed as an electron
Removing a proton from an already negative ion creates a more highly charged anion.
questions.explanation: D is correct. The growing negative charge generally makes further proton loss less favorable, contributing to Ka2<Ka1. A is incorrect: successive ionizations commonly become less favorable. B is incorrect: it still contains one acidic hydrogen in this notation. C is incorrect: acid ionization transfers a proton, not an electron.
